item.title: Oil prices post first weekly gain in November as relentless attacks raise supply worries. Will liquid gold rise further?
item.description: Crude oil price : Brent crude prices experienced a dip on Friday, yet managed to gain for the week, breaking a three-week downward trend. Renewed fears of supply disruptions in the Middle East loom large, especially following recent assaults on oil tankers and related infrastructure. Likewise, US West Texas Intermediate crude saw its own decline, having not stabilized the day before.
item.dc:creator: Veer Sharma
item.content:encoded: Brent crude prices declined on Friday but ended the week higher, snapping a three-week losing streak and recording their first weekly gain in November. Concerns over potential supply disruptions in the Middle East resurfaced after attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure.Crude oil this weekBrent crude futures fell $1.13, or 1.2%, to $95.44 a barrel on Friday. Prices touched their highest level since November 9 during the session but stayed below $100. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures settled at $83.08 a barrel, down 60 cents, or 0.7%, from Wednesday's close. There was no settlement for WTI on Thursday due to the US Thanksgiving holiday. For the week, Brent gained around 3%, while WTI declined 0.9%.Attacks on Middle Eastern energy facilities and tankers have brought supply disruption back into focus.Oil prices had come under pressure in recent weeks as markets were relieved that US President Donald Trump did not intensify military action against Iran following the midterm elections. However, Iran has continued targeting vessels passing through the strategically important Strait of Hormuz, disrupting oil exports. Yemen's Houthis have also carried out strikes on Saudi Arabian infrastructure.The US military said on Friday that it had disabled a commercial vessel on Thursday after it attempted to breach the US blockade of Iran. Meanwhile, an adviser to Iran's supreme leader said the country would keep the Strait of Hormuz closed and vowed to break the embargo, according to a Reuters report.Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery temporarily suspended some operations after being hit by a projectile on Thursday, resulting in the death of a worker, according to Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry. The incident followed attacks on key Saudi facilities, with the Houthis claiming a day earlier that they had targeted Ras Tanura, the kingdom's largest refinery and a major crude export hub.Where are prices headed?ANZ analysts Brian Martin and Daniel Hynes said Brent could still climb above $100 a barrel even without another major escalation in the Middle East. However, they said such a move would increasingly depend on evidence of actual constraints on deliverable supply, the Reuters report stated.Goldman Sachs has cautioned that the conflict could have substantial long-term consequences for global oil supplies. Earlier this month, the bank raised its oil price forecasts, warning that Brent crude could reach $140 a barrel in 2027 if Gulf production remains significantly below its 2025 average.The bank increased its December Brent price forecast to $105 a barrel from $90 previously, while its WTI projection was raised to $94 from $81. In a more bullish scenario, Brent could touch $140 a barrel and average around $130 in 2027 if oil production across the Gulf remains 3.5 million barrels per day below its 2025 average, Reuters reported, citing Goldman Sachs' projections.Goldman Sachs expects geopolitical uncertainty to contribute a larger risk premium to oil prices. Its forecasts account for the possibility of further disruptions to Middle Eastern supplies, the historical length of major supply shocks and the challenges of reaching a durable diplomatic settlement.The bank's projections underline how the eventual outcome of the conflict could shape crude prices over the longer term. In the immediate term, however, expectations of higher exports continue to act as a drag on the market.Also read: Zee Entertainment launches Re 600 crore share buyback at Rs 91 per share; Window opens December 1JPMorgan analysts have also pointed to the uncertainty surrounding the conflict and the difficulty of assessing its potential economic impact. The bank had initially expected the US administration to avoid crossing certain economic thresholds. However, seven months into the conflict, several of these thresholds have already been crossed, with no clear strategy yet in place to bring the war to an end.JPMorgan expects oil markets to remain caught between two competing forces: the possibility of further supply disruptions and the industry's ability to limit their impact.In its base-case scenario, the bank expects Middle Eastern oil supplies to stay above their 2025 average. This would be supported by measures such as ship-to-ship transfers and the use of additional pipeline capacity. At the same time, oil production growth in other parts of the world is expected to come to a standstill.Disclaimer: This article has been written by Veer Sharma, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser.
